title: Cardiovascular Embryology
subject: Cardiovascular System (CARD)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter follows the heart from paired endothelial tubes in week 3 to a four-chambered pump with separate outflow vessels, then explains the fetal circulation, the changes at birth, and the pharyngeal arch arteries that build the great vessels and set the paths of the recurrent laryngeal nerves. Part I questions usually connect three things: an embryonic structure, the adult structure it becomes, and the defect that appears when one step fails. If you understand why each step happens, you can predict the anatomy of a congenital lesion, the direction of its shunt, and its physical and ECG findings instead of memorizing each one.
prerequisites: Germ layers, gastrulation, and the somatic and splanchnic layers of lateral plate mesoderm
Cephalocaudal and lateral folding of the embryo in week 4
Gross anatomy of the adult heart chambers, septa, valves, and great vessels (CV-3)
Pressure, flow, and resistance relationships in the circulation (CV-11)
The oxygen hemoglobin dissociation curve and factors that shift it

connections.how: Adult features such as the fossa ovalis and the ligamentum arteriosum are remnants of the developmental structures described here.
Each congenital lesion in that chapter is the failure of one step of tube formation, septation, or outflow tract division explained here.
Septal defects load or displace the conduction system, which is why primum and secundum atrial septal defects produce different QRS axes.
Trisomy 21, the 22q11.2 deletion, TBX5 mutation, and ciliary dynein mutations each disrupt a specific step and so produce a predictable defect.
Pharyngeal arch remodeling explains the different loops of the two recurrent laryngeal nerves and the vulnerability of the left nerve to thoracic disease.

terms.def: The rightward (dextral or D-looping) bending of the straight heart tube during week 4 that places the future chambers in their adult positions.
An inherited, usually autosomal recessive, defect of the dynein arms or other parts of motile cilia; Kartagener syndrome is the form with situs inversus.
Mesenchymal swellings in the atrioventricular canal and outflow tract formed when endocardial cells undergo epithelial-to-mesenchymal transformation into the cardiac jelly.
The thin first atrial septum that grows from the atrial roof toward the endocardial cushions and later forms the flap valve of the foramen ovale.
The thick, incomplete second atrial septum that forms to the right of the septum primum and whose free edge bounds the foramen ovale.
The opening left by the septum secundum through which blood passes from the right to the left atrium before birth.
Neural crest cells from the hindbrain that migrate through pharyngeal arches 3, 4, and 6 into the outflow tract and help build the aorticopulmonary septum.
The spiral septum formed by fusion of the truncal ridges that divides the truncus arteriosus into the aorta and pulmonary trunk.
The fetal channel that carries umbilical venous blood through the liver to the inferior vena cava, bypassing most of the hepatic sinusoids.
The fetal vessel, derived from the left sixth arch artery, that carries blood from the pulmonary trunk to the descending aorta.
Hemoglobin of two alpha and two gamma chains that binds 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate weakly and so has a higher oxygen affinity than adult hemoglobin.
Paired arteries (aortic arches) running through each pharyngeal arch from the aortic sac to the dorsal aortae, later remodeled into the great vessels.

sections.title: Formation of the heart tube, looping, and left-right asymmetry

blocks.text: By week 3 the embryo is too large for diffusion, so the heart is the first organ to function. Cardiac progenitors pass through the cranial primitive streak into splanchnic lateral plate mesoderm and gather cranial to the neural plate as a horseshoe-shaped cardiogenic field (days 16 to 18). Endoderm signals (BMP, FGF, and Wnt inhibition) induce NKX2-5, committing them to a heart fate.

The primary heart field forms the initial tube, mainly the left ventricle and parts of the atria. The secondary heart field, in pharyngeal mesoderm, later adds most of the right ventricle and the outflow tract (conus cordis and truncus arteriosus) and part of the atria and sinus venosus. Too few secondary field cells leave the outflow tract too short to rotate and align, a cause of many outflow defects.

Angioblastic cords canalize into paired endocardial tubes, which lateral folding brings to the ventral midline to fuse into one tube by the end of week 3; cephalocaudal folding carries it into the future thorax. The tube has an inner endocardium, cardiac jelly (the future cushions), and an outer myocardium; the proepicardium later supplies the epicardium, coronary vessels, and many cardiac fibroblasts. Loss of the dorsal mesocardium leaves the transverse pericardial sinus. The heart beats at about day 22, and from caudal to cranial the tube is sinus venosus, primitive atrium, primitive ventricle, bulbus cordis, and truncus arteriosus opening into the aortic sac.

From about day 23 to 28 the tube outgrows the pericardial cavity and loops: the bulboventricular part bends ventrally, caudally, and right, and the atrial part dorsally, cranially, and left. The atria end up above and behind the ventricles, with the primitive ventricle (future left ventricle) on the left and the bulbus cordis (future right ventricle) on the right.

blocks.text: Looping direction is set at the primitive node, where dynein-driven tilted monocilia beat in a rotary fashion and move fluid to the left. This induces NODAL and LEFTY2 in left lateral plate mesoderm, midline LEFTY1 blocks spread to the right, and NODAL induces PITX2, which specifies left-sided identity of the heart, lungs, and gut.

blocks.title: Left-right signaling that directs looping

Leftward nodal flow
NODAL and LEFTY2 on the left; midline LEFTY1 barrier
PITX2 expressed on the left

blocks.caption: If nodal flow fails, the later steps still occur but on a random side.

blocks.text: In primary ciliary dyskinesia, nonfunctional dynein stops nodal flow, so sidedness is random: about half of patients have situs inversus totalis with dextrocardia (Kartagener syndrome: situs inversus, chronic sinusitis, bronchiectasis), most others have normal situs, and a minority have heterotaxy (situs ambiguus). Immotile airway cilia cause neonatal respiratory distress, wet cough, otitis media, and bronchiectasis; immotile sperm flagella cause male infertility, and poor tubal transport raises ectopic pregnancy risk.

Risk depends on whether heart and body agree about sidedness: mirror-image dextrocardia keeps connections concordant, so the heart is usually normal; dextrocardia with normal abdominal situs or heterotaxy (often asplenia or polysplenia) carries a high risk of complex lesions. Mirror-image dextrocardia inverts P, QRS, and T in lead I and gives diminishing precordial R waves.

sections.title: Atrial septation and atrial septal defects

blocks.text: Before birth, oxygenated blood must cross from the right to the left atrium; after birth the atria must be sealed. Two incomplete, overlapping septa with offset openings solve this by acting as a one-way flap valve.

blocks.title: Atrial septation
steps: Septum primum grows toward the cushions; gap below is the ostium primum
Apoptosis in the upper septum primum opens the ostium secundum
Septum primum fuses with the cushions; ostium primum closes
Thick septum secundum grows down on the right side
Its free edge leaves the foramen ovale
Lower septum primum acts as the flap valve; flow is right to left
After birth the flap is pressed shut; fusion leaves the fossa ovalis
blocks.caption: The ostium secundum is a hole in the septum primum; the foramen ovale is the gap left by the septum secundum.

blocks.text: Cushion tissue closes the ostium primum at the end of week 5. Because the thin septum primum lies on the left and the rigid septum secundum on the right with nonaligned openings, blood crosses only right to left: higher fetal right atrial pressure pushes the flap open, and after birth higher left atrial pressure presses it shut (section C06). The floor of the adult fossa ovalis is septum primum, and its rim (limbus) is the edge of the septum secundum.

Anatomic fusion takes months and fails in about a quarter of adults, leaving a patent foramen ovale (PFO). No tissue is missing, so blood crosses only when right atrial pressure transiently exceeds left, as on release of a Valsalva strain, with coughing, or with acute pulmonary hypertension from pulmonary embolism. A venous thrombus can then reach the systemic arteries (paradoxical embolism) and cause a stroke.

An atrial septal defect (ASD) is a true tissue deficiency. Because the right ventricle is more compliant, blood shunts left to right, volume loading the right heart and lungs but not the left ventricle. The secundum ASD, the most common, lies at the fossa ovalis and results from excess resorption of the septum primum or a deficient septum secundum; TBX5 (Holt-Oram syndrome, with upper limb defects) and NKX2-5 (with AV conduction disease) mutations are known causes. Primum and sinus venosus defects are compared in the table in section C03.

The small interatrial pressure difference makes flow across the defect nearly silent. The murmur is a systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border from increased flow across a normal pulmonary valve, with a mid-diastolic tricuspid flow rumble when the shunt is large. The ECG shows right axis deviation and an rsR prime pattern in V1. Over decades, high pulmonary flow can remodel the arterioles, raise resistance, and reverse the shunt with cyanosis (Eisenmenger syndrome), a possible end stage of any large left-to-right shunt.

blocks.title: Why S2 is widely and fixedly split in ASD
blocks.text: Normally inspiration increases right heart return, prolongs right ventricular ejection, delays pulmonic closure (P2), and widens the split. In an ASD the right ventricle receives systemic return plus the shunt every beat, so P2 is always late and the split is wide. In inspiration the extra systemic return raises right atrial pressure and shrinks the left-to-right shunt by about the same amount; in expiration the reverse occurs. The atria act as one chamber, so right ventricular filling and P2 timing barely change with respiration. A right bundle branch block delays P2 electrically, so its wide split still varies with breathing.

blocks.predict: A fetal foramen ovale closes prematurely in mid-gestation. Which side of the heart is underdeveloped at birth?
blocks.explain: The left side. Most left atrial and left ventricular filling in the fetus arrives through the foramen ovale because pulmonary venous return is small. Without it the left heart receives little flow and grows poorly, while the right heart enlarges. Embryonic chambers grow in proportion to the flow through them.
blocks.check: Compare with the one-way flap valve and the fetal circulation in section C05.

sections.title: Endocardial cushions, the atrioventricular canal, and AV septal defects

blocks.text: A single atrioventricular (AV) canal opens mainly over the future left ventricle. It must shift right and divide into tricuspid and mitral orifices. The endocardial cushions do both and, sitting at the center of the heart, also build the lower atrial and upper ventricular septa, so one cushion defect damages several structures.

At the end of week 4, AV canal and outflow myocardium signals the endocardium (TGF-beta and BMP families). Endocardial cells undergo epithelial-to-mesenchymal transformation, losing their junctions and invading the cardiac jelly. Superior and inferior AV cushions form, with smaller lateral cushions; the outflow ridges form separately and receive neural crest cells (section C04). In week 5 the superior and inferior cushions fuse, dividing the canal into right and left orifices. The fused mass closes the ostium primum (lowest atrial septum), and inferior cushion tissue joins the conal ridges and muscular septum to close the interventricular foramen as the membranous septum by about the end of week 7. Cushion mesenchyme around each orifice is undermined on its ventricular side; the muscular strands left behind become chordae tendineae (muscle replaced by dense connective tissue) and papillary muscles. The left orifice gets two leaflets and the right three.

The muscular ventricular septum forms as the expanding ventricles press their medial walls together. The membranous septum closes last and needs three tissue sources to meet, so most ventricular septal defects (VSDs) are perimembranous; muscular VSDs, sometimes multiple, are less common, and small ones often close.

Failure of cushion fusion produces an atrioventricular septal defect (AVSD, AV canal defect). The complete form has a primum ASD above an inlet VSD with one common five-leaflet AV valve. The partial form has two orifices but a primum ASD and a cleft anterior mitral leaflet with mitral regurgitation. In the complete form the VSD transmits left ventricular pressure to the pulmonary arteries, so high flow and high pressure cause heart failure within months and earlier pulmonary vascular disease than an isolated ASD. The AV node and His bundle are displaced inferiorly and posteriorly and the left anterior fascicle is short, giving left (superior) axis deviation, often with first degree AV block.

blocks.text: About 40 to 50% of children with trisomy 21 have congenital heart disease, and AVSD, especially the complete form, is the characteristic lesion; a large share of complete AVSDs occur in Down syndrome. The extra chromosome is thought to disturb cushion cell adhesion, migration, and matrix, though the genes are not fully established. VSD, secundum ASD, PDA, and tetralogy are also more frequent.

In Ebstein anomaly the septal and posterior tricuspid leaflets are poorly undermined, so their attachment is displaced toward the apex, part of the right ventricle is atrialized, and the valve leaks. In tricuspid atresia the right AV orifice is obliterated, so right atrial blood must cross the atrial septum, the hypoplastic right ventricle fills through a VSD, and the lungs are supplied through that VSD or the ductus.

sections.title: Neural crest, the aorticopulmonary septum, and conotruncal defects

blocks.text: The single outflow tract must become a pulmonary trunk leaving the right ventricle anteriorly and to the left and an aorta leaving the left ventricle posteriorly and to the right. Cardiac neural crest cells from the hindbrain migrate through pharyngeal arches 3, 4, and 6; some support the arch arteries and help form the thymus and parathyroids, and others populate the truncal and conal ridges and the semilunar valves. Removing this crest in animal embryos produces persistent truncus arteriosus.

In week 5 the right superior and left inferior truncal ridges grow distally while swinging around the truncal wall, so when they fuse the aorticopulmonary septum twists about 180 degrees. The right dorsal and left ventral conal ridges fuse into the conal (outlet) septum, which separates the right ventricular infundibulum from the aortic vestibule and meets the muscular septum and inferior cushion to complete the membranous septum. Because outlet and ventricular septa must align, displacing one affects both.

blocks.title: Conotruncal defects and the step that failed
rows: Truncal ridges fail to form or fuse
One trunk and valve over a VSD, giving coronary, pulmonary, and systemic arteries
Mixing with mild cyanosis; excess pulmonary flow and heart failure as resistance falls
Aorta from right ventricle, pulmonary trunk from left ventricle
Parallel circuits; survival requires mixing (foramen ovale, ductus, VSD); severe early cyanosis; narrow pedicle; maternal diabetes
Anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular septum
Pulmonary stenosis, malalignment VSD, overriding aorta, right ventricular hypertrophy
Right-to-left shunt set by outflow obstruction; hypercyanotic spells; boot-shaped heart
blocks.caption: No septum, a straight septum, and a displaced septum produce the three classic conotruncal defects.

blocks.text: In transposition the circuits run in parallel, so cyanosis appears within hours to days and worsens as the ductus closes; the great vessels lie one in front of the other, narrowing the vascular pedicle. In tetralogy, unequal division of the conus explains all four features: the narrow infundibulum causes pulmonary stenosis, the misplaced outlet septum leaves a malalignment VSD, the enlarged aortic outflow overrides it, and right ventricular hypertrophy follows from the obstruction.

Because the VSD is large, both ventricles share systolic pressure, and shunt direction depends on right ventricular outflow resistance versus systemic resistance; mild obstruction gives a mostly left-to-right shunt and a pink child. The murmur comes from the narrowed outflow tract, so it softens during a spell. The radiograph shows a boot-shaped heart (raised apex, concave upper left border), and chronic hypoxemia causes secondary polycythemia and clubbing.

blocks.title: Hypercyanotic (tet) spell and relief by squatting
steps: Crying or exertion lowers systemic resistance
Right outflow resistance rises relative to systemic
More blood shunts right to left; pulmonary flow falls
Hypoxemia and acidosis lower systemic resistance further
Squatting kinks femoral arteries and raises systemic resistance, breaking the cycle
blocks.caption: Anything that lowers systemic resistance worsens cyanosis in tetralogy, and anything that raises it improves cyanosis.

blocks.text: The 22q11.2 deletion (DiGeorge or velocardiofacial syndrome) removes one copy of TBX1 and neighbors, disrupting the pharyngeal tissue through which crest cells migrate. Outflow defects (truncus arteriosus, tetralogy, interrupted aortic arch) arrive with thymic hypoplasia and T cell deficiency, parathyroid hypoplasia with hypocalcemia, and facial and palatal anomalies. Excess retinoic acid, as with maternal isotretinoin, disturbs crest migration and causes conotruncal and craniofacial defects.

blocks.predict: A newborn with D-transposition, a small foramen ovale, and no VSD is pink at birth but deeply cyanotic on day 2. What changed?
blocks.explain: The ductus arteriosus closed. With parallel circuits, oxygenated blood reaches the body only through the interatrial opening, the ductus, or a VSD. When rising O2 and falling prostaglandin E2 constricted the ductus, mixing depended on a small foramen ovale alone and systemic oxygen delivery collapsed.
blocks.check: Compare with transposition above and with ductal closure in section C06.

sections.title: Fetal circulation and delivery of the best-oxygenated blood to the brain

blocks.text: The fetus exchanges gases in the placenta, so its circulation runs in parallel: both ventricles pump into the systemic circuit, three shunts bypass the liver and lungs, and streaming sends the best-oxygenated blood to the heart and brain.

Fetal pulmonary vascular resistance is high because the lungs are fluid filled and their vessels compressed, low alveolar PO2 causes hypoxic vasoconstriction, and mediators favor constriction (high endothelin, low nitric oxide). The placenta is a large low-resistance circuit that keeps systemic resistance low. Pulmonary trunk pressure therefore exceeds descending aortic pressure, and most right ventricular output crosses the ductus arteriosus; only a small fraction of combined output passes through the lungs.

blocks.title: Path of blood through the fetal circulation
steps: Umbilical vein brings the best blood (about 80% saturated)
Ductus venosus shunts part of it past the liver into the IVC
Crista dividens streams IVC blood through the foramen ovale
Left ventricle ejects; coronary, carotid, and subclavian arteries branch first
SVC blood goes right atrium to right ventricle to pulmonary trunk
Most pulmonary trunk flow crosses the ductus to the descending aorta
Umbilical arteries return blood (about 60% saturated) to the placenta
blocks.caption: IVC blood goes to the left heart and the brain; SVC blood goes to the right heart, the ductus, and the lower body.

blocks.text: The umbilical vein is the most saturated fetal vessel (about 80%, yet with a PO2 of only about 30 to 35 mmHg). Part of its flow enters the hepatic sinusoids through the left portal vein, and the rest passes through the ductus venosus, whose inlet regulates the bypass and protects the heart from sudden volume loads such as during uterine contractions. In the right atrium the lower edge of the septum secundum (crista dividens) and the IVC valve direct the better-oxygenated stream across the foramen ovale. It is diluted only slightly by the small pulmonary venous return before the left ventricle ejects it.

Desaturated SVC blood, with coronary sinus blood and part of the IVC stream, enters the right ventricle. The right ventricle supplies slightly more than half of combined output, which is why both ventricles have similar wall thickness at birth. Its output enters the aorta through the ductus distal to the left subclavian artery, so the myocardium and brain receive left ventricular blood before it mixes with desaturated ductal blood, while the lower body receives the mixture. The umbilical arteries, branches of the internal iliac arteries, return blood to the placenta.

Fetal tissues are well oxygenated despite low PO2. HbF binds 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate weakly because the gamma chain has serine where the beta chain has a 2,3-BPG-binding histidine (position 143), so its P50 is about 19 mmHg versus about 27 mmHg for adult hemoglobin. The fetus also has a higher hemoglobin concentration and a high cardiac output for its mass. In the placenta, the double Bohr effect helps: fetal blood loses CO2 and gains affinity, while maternal blood gains CO2 and loses affinity.

sections.title: Circulatory changes at birth and remnants of fetal vessels

blocks.text: At birth the circulation changes from parallel to series. The first breaths expand the alveoli and raise alveolar PO2, relieving hypoxic vasoconstriction, and O2 and shear stress release nitric oxide and prostacyclin, so pulmonary resistance falls and flow rises several-fold. Cord clamping removes the low-resistance placenta and raises systemic resistance.

Increased pulmonary venous return raises left atrial pressure while loss of umbilical return lowers right atrial pressure, so the septum primum is pressed against the septum secundum and the foramen ovale closes functionally within minutes to hours (section C02).

Across the ductus the gradient reverses, so flow briefly runs aorta to pulmonary trunk. Rising arterial PO2 constricts ductal smooth muscle, partly because O2-sensitive K+ channels close, the membrane depolarizes, and L-type Ca2+ channels open. Prostaglandin E2 falls because the placenta is gone and the perfused lungs metabolize it; in the fetus PGE2 acting on EP receptors raised cAMP and kept the muscle relaxed. Functional closure occurs within 1 to 3 days in term infants; intimal thickening and fibrosis over weeks leave the ligamentum arteriosum. Cyclooxygenase inhibition promotes closure and a PGE analog keeps the ductus open, confirming the mechanism. The umbilical arteries constrict within minutes to mechanical, thermal, and O2 stimuli; the umbilical vein and ductus venosus close slightly later, and liver perfusion then comes from the portal vein and hepatic artery.

blocks.text: A patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) is most common in prematurity, because immature ductal muscle responds less to O2 and more to PGE2; congenital rubella and high altitude also predispose. Aortic pressure exceeds pulmonary pressure throughout the cycle, giving a continuous machinery murmur below the left clavicle, and diastolic runoff widens pulse pressure. The shunt volume loads the left heart. Ductal closure unmasks ductus-dependent lesions: transposition (mixing), pulmonary atresia (lung supply), and hypoplastic left heart or critical coarctation (systemic supply). In persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn, resistance stays high and blood shunts right to left through the foramen ovale and ductus despite normal anatomy.

blocks.title: Differential cyanosis in a long-standing PDA
blocks.text: A large PDA first shunts aorta to pulmonary artery. Years of high flow and pressure remodel the pulmonary arterioles until pulmonary pressure exceeds aortic pressure and the shunt reverses (Eisenmenger physiology). The ductus enters the aorta distal to the left subclavian artery, so the head and arms still receive unmixed left ventricular blood while the descending aorta carries desaturated blood to the lower body. The toes are cyanotic and clubbed while the fingers stay pink. A reversed VSD or ASD mixes blood before the aorta, so fingers and toes are equally cyanotic.

sections.title: Pharyngeal arch arteries and the recurrent laryngeal nerves

blocks.text: Each pharyngeal arch artery runs from the aortic sac to the paired dorsal aortae, which fuse caudally into one descending aorta. The arteries appear craniocaudally in weeks 4 and 5, are never all present together, and are remodeled by selective persistence and regression into the asymmetric adult pattern.

rows: Right horn: brachiocephalic trunk; left horn: arch up to the left common carotid
Part of the maxillary artery; hyoid and stapedial arteries (largely regress)

Arch between the left common carotid and left subclavian arteries
Proximal right subclavian artery (distal part from right dorsal aorta and seventh intersegmental artery)
Proximal right and left pulmonary arteries; distal left becomes the ductus arteriosus, distal right regresses
Descending aorta beyond the left subclavian
blocks.caption: The dorsal aorta between the third and fourth arches disappears on both sides, and the right dorsal aorta regresses below the right seventh intersegmental artery.

blocks.text: The vagus supplies the fourth arch through the superior laryngeal nerve (cricothyroid) and the sixth arch through the recurrent laryngeal nerve (all other intrinsic laryngeal muscles). Each recurrent nerve first hooks under its sixth arch artery, and as the heart descends the nerves are dragged caudally around the lowest persisting arch vessel. On the right the distal sixth arch artery and the fifth regress, so the nerve slides up to the right subclavian artery (fourth arch) at the root of the neck. On the left the distal sixth arch persists as the ductus, so the nerve stays under the aortic arch just behind the ligamentum arteriosum in the superior mediastinum. Both ascend in the tracheoesophageal groove.

The recurrent nerve supplies the posterior cricoarytenoid, the only vocal fold abductor, so injury leaves the fold near the midline with hoarseness. The left nerve's thoracic course near the aortic arch, left pulmonary artery, left main bronchus, and hilar nodes makes hoarseness a sign of aortic arch aneurysm, left hilar or mediastinal tumor or nodes, a dilated left atrium or pulmonary artery (cardiovocal or Ortner syndrome), or PDA ligation. The right nerve is vulnerable at the neck root to an apical lung tumor or subclavian aneurysm. Both are at risk in thyroid surgery.

If the right fourth arch artery and cranial right dorsal aorta regress while the caudal right dorsal aorta persists, the right subclavian becomes the last arch branch and crosses behind the esophagus (aberrant right subclavian artery), which can cause dysphagia; with no right fourth arch vessel to hold it, the right laryngeal nerve does not recur (nonrecurrent laryngeal nerve). Persistence of the right dorsal aorta gives a double aortic arch, a vascular ring that can compress the trachea and esophagus. Abnormal regression of the left fourth arch artery interrupts the arch between the left common carotid and left subclavian arteries, so the lower body depends on a PDA; because neural crest supports the fourth arch artery, this type is most strongly linked to the 22q11.2 deletion.

blocks.predict: A 60-year-old with long-standing mitral stenosis develops hoarseness. Which nerve is involved, and what developmental fact explains why only one side is at risk?
blocks.explain: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve. A large left atrium and dilated pulmonary artery compress it against the aortic arch and ligamentum arteriosum. Only the left nerve passes there, because the left distal sixth arch artery persisted as the ductus and held the nerve in the thorax, while on the right it regressed and the nerve rose to the subclavian artery.

integration.text: The adult heart records its development. Splanchnic mesoderm forms the tube, endocardium becomes the cushions that build the valves and central septa, and hindbrain neural crest divides the outflow tract and supports the arch arteries, so the fossa ovalis is septum primum, the membranous septum and valve leaflets are cushion tissue, and the ligamentum arteriosum marks the left sixth arch artery. Physiology explains the shunts: each runs along a gradient created by high pulmonary resistance and a low-resistance placenta, HbF and the double Bohr effect favor placental O2 transfer, and O2-sensitive channels and PGE2 control the ductus. ECG findings follow the conduction anatomy of CV-7: right ventricular volume load in secundum ASD and a displaced AV node in AVSD.

Genetics and pathology tie the heart to other systems: trisomy 21 disrupts the cushions, 22q11.2 deletion links outflow defects to T cell deficiency and hypocalcemia, TBX5 and NKX2-5 link septal defects to limb and conduction abnormalities, and ciliary dynein defects link organ position to sinusitis and infertility. Maternal diabetes, rubella, and retinoic acid act on the same steps. Most defects have no recognized cause, and real lesions vary in severity.

summary: Splanchnic mesoderm forms paired endocardial tubes that fuse into one heart tube by the end of week 3; it beats by about day 22 and loops right during days 23 to 28.

Dynein-driven leftward nodal flow activates NODAL and PITX2 on the left; ciliary dynein defects randomize sidedness, giving situs inversus in about half (Kartagener syndrome) with sinusitis, bronchiectasis, and infertility.
The ostium secundum is a hole in the septum primum, the foramen ovale is the gap left by the septum secundum, and the septum primum is the one-way flap valve.
A PFO is an unsealed flap that allows paradoxical embolism; a secundum ASD is a true deficiency with right heart volume loading, right axis deviation, and a fixed split S2.

Fused endocardial cushions divide the AV canal, close the ostium primum, help form the membranous septum, and form the AV valves; their failure gives AVSD with left axis deviation, typical of trisomy 21.
Most VSDs are perimembranous because the membranous septum closes last and needs three tissue sources to meet.

Cardiac neural crest builds the spiral aorticopulmonary septum: no septum gives truncus arteriosus, a straight septum gives transposition, and a displaced infundibular septum gives tetralogy of Fallot.
Fetal shunts bypass the liver and lungs, and streaming plus ductal entry distal to the head vessels deliver the best-oxygenated blood to the heart and brain.
At birth falling pulmonary resistance raises left atrial pressure and closes the foramen ovale, while rising O2 and falling PGE2 constrict the ductus arteriosus.
The right recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the right subclavian (fourth arch); the left loops under the aortic arch at the ligamentum arteriosum (sixth arch), giving it a long thoracic course.

verify: Developmental timings (cardiogenic field days 16 to 18, first heartbeat about day 22, looping days 23 to 28, ostium primum closed at the end of week 5, membranous septum closed by the end of week 7) vary by a few days between texts.

Derivation of the trabeculated right ventricle is given here as the proximal bulbus cordis (Langman); several review books instead attribute the trabeculated parts of both ventricles to the primitive ventricle. Confirm which version NABNE expects.

Prevalence figures are approximate: PFO in about 25% of adults (quoted from about 20 to 30%), congenital heart disease in about 40 to 50% of children with trisomy 21, and about half of primary ciliary dyskinesia patients with situs inversus.

Fetal values (umbilical vein about 80% saturated and PO2 about 30 to 35 mmHg, umbilical arteries about 60%, HbF P50 about 19 mmHg, ductus venosus fraction of umbilical flow about 20 to 30% in human Doppler studies) come from mixed human and animal data and differ slightly between sources.
Timing of anatomic fusion of the foramen ovale (months, often stated as within the first year) and of functional ductal closure (1 to 3 days in term infants) varies between sources.

The mechanism of O2-induced ductal constriction (inhibition of O2-sensitive K+ channels with Ca2+ entry) is well supported experimentally but is described only in general terms in some standard texts.
Confirm whether NABNE Part I expects the eponyms Holt-Oram, Ebstein, Ortner (cardiovocal syndrome), Eisenmenger, and DiGeorge, or only descriptive terms.

Requested new diagram names for a future revision: atrial-septation (four panels from septum primum to fossa ovalis), fetal-circulation (labeled shunts with relative saturations), and aortic-arches (arch artery derivatives with both recurrent laryngeal nerve loops).
